claim: Shale porosity from sonic: phi = 1 - (delta t_ma/delta t)^(1/x) with delta t_ma = 220 microseconds/m and x = 2.19 (Issler 1992).
quote: We used the values of delta t_ma = 220 microseconds/m and x = 2.19 proposed by Issler (1992) for low total organic carbon, noncalcareous shales.

claim: Hydrostatic gradient assumed 10.5 MPa/km; lithostatic from the integrated density log.
quote: We assumed a hydrostatic pressure gradient of 10.5 MPa/km and calculated the lithostatic pressure gradient by integrating the density log.

claim: Sonic-derived shale porosities are within 5 % of sidewall core values except three points at 2100-2200 m.
quote: Shale porosity values from the Pathfinder well calculated with equation 4 are within 5% of the measured values, except for three points between 2100 and 2200 m (Fig. 3).

claim: Porosity decreases gradually to about 2000 m, then increases below the B fault and levels off below 2130 m.
quote: In general, the porosity decreases gradually from the top of the well to about 2000 m. Below the B fault, porosity begins to increase before leveling out below 2130 m.

claim: Predicted overpressure rises from 8 to 15 MPa below the D fault and stays at 15 MPa below the A fault; the prediction is 3-5 MPa low below the D fault.
quote: Below the D fault, predicted overpressures increase from 8 to 15 MPa, and remain at 15 MPa below the A fault.

claim: Measured fluid pressure reaches 93 % of lithostatic beneath the A fault: P_f = 42.2 MPa, P_l = 45.2 MPa at 2197 m.
quote: Measured fluid pressures approach 93% of lithostatic pressure immediately beneath the A fault zone (Pf = 42.2 MPa, Pl = 45.2 MPa at 2197 m).

claim: A second curve with beta = 7.2 x 10^-2 MPa^-1 matches pressures at depth but overpredicts them higher in the section.
quote: Second curve (beta = 7.2 x 10^-2 MPa^-1) matches pressures at depth, but significantly overpredicts pressures higher in section.

claim: Compaction is irreversible: when effective stress falls, porosity follows a near-horizontal unloading curve that Eq. 1 does not describe.
quote: As the effective stress decreases, sediment porosity follows a path below the normal compaction curve known as an unloading curve (Fig. 4D, lower) that is approximately horizontal except at very low effective stresses (Karig and Hou, 1992). Equation 1 does not describe the porosity-stress evolution of this unloading curve.
